pronunciation.note: Kannon is Tier 2: the Japanese form loses the long ā and special ś of the Sanskrit. The name's power is devotional and artistic, not orthographic.

domains.title: Perceiver of the World's Cries
domains.subtitle: Compassion, Mercy, and Salvation
domains.lead: Kannon is the Japanese form of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of infinite compassion. Kannon hears the cries of all beings and responds in whatever form is needed — male or female, one-faced or thousand-armed, gentle or wrathful. Kannon is one of the most beloved Buddhist figures in Japan, worshipped at pilgrimage sites from Kyōto's Kiyomizu-dera to the island sanctuary of Kannonzaki.

mythology.lead: Kannon's mythology is drawn from Indian, Chinese, and Japanese Buddhist sources. The figure embodies the vow to postpone buddhahood until all beings are saved.

myths.title: The Vow of Avalokiteśvara
myths.text: The Lotus Sutra's 'Universal Gate' chapter describes Avalokiteśvara's vow to save all beings from fire, flood, prison, demons, and despair. Those who call the name will be heard, regardless of their condition. This chapter became the foundation of Kannon devotion across East Asia.

myths.title: Guānyīn Becomes Kannon
myths.text: In China, Avalokiteśvara gradually took on female forms and became Guānyīn, a goddess of mercy and childbirth. In Japan this figure became Kannon, who could appear as male or female depending on the needs of the devotee. The shift reflects the bodhisattva's promise to assume any form.

myths.title: The Saikoku Circuit
myths.text: The Saikoku thirty-three Kannon pilgrimage circuit, established by the 12th century, links temples across the Kansai region. Pilgrims travel between them seeking healing, safe childbirth, and salvation. Kannon's compassionate presence is understood to extend across the entire landscape.

lore.syncretism: Kannon absorbed native kami functions, especially those related to water, childbirth, and protection at sea. Shrine-Buddhist synthesis (shinbutsu shūgō) produced hybrid figures such as Kannon as a local kami, and hidden Christians (kakure kirishitan) disguised the Virgin Mary as Kannon statues. The bodhisattva's flexibility made Kannon a bridge between religious worlds.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kannon is one of the most common figures in Japanese art and worship. The Great Buddha of Kamakura is Amida, but Kannon statues rival it in number and devotion. Kannonzaki, Kiyomizu-dera, and Hase-dera are famous pilgrimage sites, and the name Kannon appears in place names, festivals, and personal names across Japan.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kannon is the promise that no cry is unheard. The bodhisattva does not ask us to become perfect before receiving help; compassion arrives in the very moment of suffering. To call on Kannon is to trust that the world is not indifferent.
lore.archaeology: Kiyomizu-dera in Kyōto and Hase-dera in Kamakura are among the most famous Kannon temples in Japan, preserving Heian- and Kamakura-period sculpture and architecture. The Saikoku and Bandō pilgrimage circuits link dozens of temples with Kannon statuary, votive materials, and pilgrimage culture.
